name: Alexander (son of Simon of Cyrene)
title: Son of Simon of Cyrene
summary: Alexander is mentioned as the son of Simon of Cyrene, the man who was compelled to carry Jesus' cross on the way to Golgotha. Together with his brother Rufus, he is named in Mark 15:21 – a detail that is unusual in the gospel narratives. The fact that Mark specifically names these two sons is usually interpreted as a sign that they were well-known figures among the original readers of the gospel. Several scholars have linked this to the church in Rome, but there are also other theories about who the recipients were. Beyond this single reference, we have no certain information about Alexander's later life, and it is not possible to identify him with other persons named Alexander in the New Testament.
roles: Presumed member of the early Christian church

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as son of Simon of Cyrene
keyEvents.description: In connection with Jesus' journey to Golgotha, the Gospel of Mark notes that Simon of Cyrene, who was forced to carry the cross, was the father of Alexander and Rufus. The fact that these two are named explicitly is remarkable and suggests they were recognizable to the earliest readers of the gospel.

versions.summary: Alexander was the son of Simon of Cyrene, the man forced to carry Jesus' cross to Golgotha. He is mentioned alongside his brother Rufus in the Gospel of Mark, indicating that the family became known in the early Christian church. The fact that Mark names the sons suggests they were familiar to the first readers of the gospel.
versions.title: Son of the cross-bearer
versions.reason: [major] There is no biblical source confirming that Alexander was a disciple. Mark 15:21 mentions him only by name as the son of Simon of Cyrene. The fact that he was known in the early church does not necessarily mean he was a disciple. The role should be changed to something more neutral, such as 'member of the early Christian community,' or removed in favor of a more sober description.; [minor] The title 'Son of the Cross-Bearer' is poetic and descriptive but could be made slightly more precise by including that he is the son of Simon of Cyrene for clarity.; [minor] The second key event ('The Father's Role in Jesus' Passion Story') primarily concerns Simon of Cyrene, not Alexander himself. Verse 22 deals with the arrival at Golgotha and is not directly relevant to Alexander. The event should either be tightened or removed, as it duplicates information that belongs on Simon's profile.; [minor] The summary is good but should avoid implying discipleship without evidence. The phrasing 'known in the early Christian community' is sound but should clarify that this is a conclusion drawn from Mark mentioning their names.; [major] Footnotes are missing. There are several interesting historical, linguistic, and theological details that should be covered—for example, why Mark names the sons, the connection to Rufus in Romans 16:13, and Cyrene as a Jewish diaspora community in North Africa.

versions.summary: Alexander was the son of Simon of Cyrene, the man forced to carry Jesus' cross to Golgotha. He is mentioned alongside his brother Rufus in the Gospel of Mark (Mark 15:21), suggesting the family was known among early Christians. The fact that Mark specifically names the sons is unusual in gospel texts and implies they were well-known figures to the first readers of the gospel, likely the church in Rome. Beyond this reference, we know nothing certain about Alexander's life or ministry.
versions.title: Son of Simon of Cyrene
versions.reason: [minor] The era is set to 'early-church', but Alexander is primarily known from an event during Jesus' crucifixion. 'Jesus' could have been an alternative, but since he is assumed to have been active in the early church and that is where his significance lies, 'early-church' is defensible. Keep as it is.; [minor] The role "member of the early Christian community" is a reasonable inference, but strictly speaking, the Bible does not explicitly confirm that Alexander was a Christian. The text implies this indirectly by naming him for the readers, but it remains an interpretation. A more precise formulation could have been "assumed member of the early Christian community".; [minor] The summary is good, but the phrase "probably the church in Rome" is a widespread but not universally accepted hypothesis. It could be made slightly more nuanced to reflect that this is a common but not certain assumption.

footnotes.text: The fact that Mark names Alexander and Rufus as sons of Simon of Cyrene (Mark 15:21) is unusual in gospel texts. Most scholars interpret this as a sign that the brothers were known in the Christian community for which the Gospel of Mark was originally written. A widespread theory links this to the church in Rome, but other target audiences have also been proposed.

Cyrene (modern-day Libya) had a significant Jewish community in antiquity. According to both Josephus and archaeological findings, there was a large Jewish population there, and Jews from Cyrene had their own synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9). Simon was likely a diaspora Jew who came to Jerusalem for the Passover celebration.

Many scholars have suggested a connection between the Rufus mentioned in Mark 15:21 and the Rufus mentioned in Romans 16:13, where Paul greets 'Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has also been a mother to me.' If this is the same person, it strengthens the theory that the family became prominent in the Roman church.

The name Alexander (Greek: Ἀλέξανδρος) was very common among Hellenistic Jews in the diaspora and indicates the family's connection to Greco-Roman culture. The name means 'defender of the people' and was widespread after the conquests of Alexander the Great.

It is worth noting that the name Alexander appears several times in the New Testament (e.g., Acts 4:6; Acts 19:33; 1 Timothy 1:20; 2 Timothy 4:14), but there are no certain grounds for identifying any of these with Simon of Cyrene's sons. The name's widespread use makes such identifications uncertain.
